paragraphs: The paper explains policy gradient methods through two repeated operations. The first improves a policy, meaning the rule an agent uses to choose actions. The second finds the best approximation to that improved policy within the policies the model can actually represent. This separates the goal of improving behavior from the constraint of expressing that behavior with a particular model.

Using this framework, the authors construct operator-based versions of REINFORCE and PPO. These versions provide a way to understand their original counterparts through the roles played by improvement and projection. The paper also uses that understanding to propose a new global lower bound on expected return, the quantity that summarizes the reward a policy is expected to earn.

The broader contribution is a connection between methods centered on policies and methods centered on values. In particular, the framework relates REINFORCE to the Bellman optimality operator. It offers a common mathematical perspective on approaches that are usually presented through different update rules.
neurips-2020-an-operator-view-of-policy-.tldr: The paper separates policy gradient learning into improvement and projection operations, connecting policy-based and value-based methods.

paragraphs: This paper builds a probabilistic document model around the organization of words into sentences and sentences into documents. Word-level convolutions capture topics expressed through phrases, while stochastic transitions model how topic usage changes between consecutive sentences. Aggregating the topic proportions of individual sentences produces a representation of the whole document.

The bidirectional version lets information travel both forward and backward through the sentence sequence. Consequently, a sentence representation can incorporate context from sentences on either side. This extends the model beyond describing topic progression in only one direction while retaining representations at several levels of the document.

For efficient inference, the authors combine a convolutional-recurrent network with a hybrid of stochastic-gradient MCMC and amortized variational inference. Across multiple document collections, they report interpretable phrase topics and sentence transitions, along with document features useful for distinguishing categories. The models achieve state-of-the-art document categorization performance in the reported experiments while remaining efficient in memory and computation.
neurips-2020-bidirectional-convolutional.tldr: A hierarchical probabilistic model combines phrase topics and bidirectional sentence transitions to learn interpretable, effective document representations.

paragraphs: A classifier can express uncertainty by returning a set of possible labels. This paper develops methods for constructing such sets when labels are categorical and have no natural ordering. It specializes conformal inference, cross-validation+, and jackknife+, techniques that can work with virtually any machine learning algorithm and provide guarantees about how often prediction sets contain the correct answer.

The central contribution is a new conformity score, which determines how well a candidate label agrees with the information used to build a prediction set. The authors design this score specifically for classification. Their methods preserve guaranteed marginal coverage, a guarantee averaged across the data distribution, while adapting to complex distributions.

The adaptation claim concerns favorable approximate conditional coverage compared with alternatives: coverage that better reflects different parts of the distribution. It does not replace the marginal guarantee with an exact conditional one. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the practical usefulness of the guarantees and show statistical advantages over existing methods.
neurips-2020-classification-with-valid-a.tldr: A new classification conformity score produces prediction sets with guaranteed marginal coverage and improved adaptation to complex data distributions.

paragraphs: AGS-CL addresses learning a sequence of tasks by managing which neural network nodes remain available for learning and which are protected. It assigns importance to nodes and updates those importance values after each task. Two penalties based on group sparsity are then applied selectively according to that importance, making the treatment of a node depend on its role in previous learning.

The optimization method is a central part of the design. Using proximal gradient descent guarantees exact sparsity and freezing during learning, giving the method explicit control over model capacity. After each task, it also reinitializes weights associated with unimportant nodes. The authors use this step to support efficient learning and prevent negative transfer from earlier tasks.

Experiments cover representative benchmarks in both supervised learning and reinforcement learning. The authors report significant improvements over several state-of-the-art baselines. They also report orders of magnitude less memory for storing regularization parameters, a specific storage advantage rather than a claim about every component of training memory.
neurips-2020-continual-learning-with-nod.tldr: AGS-CL uses adaptive node importance, sparsity, and freezing to manage continual learning while greatly reducing regularization-parameter storage.

paragraphs: This paper improves single-image super-resolution by exploiting patterns that recur at different scales within the same image. Existing deep non-local methods commonly search for similar patches at one scale. The authors argue that this leaves useful detail cues unused: a pattern appearing at another scale can provide information relevant to reconstructing a low-resolution patch.

Their internal graph neural network constructs connections dynamically. For each patch in the input, it searches for nearby matches in a downsampled version of that image. It then takes the corresponding patches from the original input, which have higher resolution relative to those matches, and adaptively combines their information using the graph's edge labels.

This transfers detail from image-specific examples to the patch being reconstructed. Those internal low- and high-resolution relationships complement information learned from the external training dataset. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach against state-of-the-art super-resolution methods, including existing non-local networks, supporting the value of searching across scales.
neurips-2020-cross-scale-internal-graph-.tldr: A graph network uses recurring patches across image scales to supply image-specific detail cues for super-resolution.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what contrastive self-supervised image models actually learn to ignore. These models treat an image and its augmented versions as belonging together. The authors examine whether the resulting representations remain stable under changes that matter for recognition, rather than treating strong downstream performance as evidence that all useful invariances have been learned.

Their experiments show that MOCO and PIRL learn representations resistant to occlusion, but fail to capture viewpoint invariance and invariance across different instances of a category. They also find that access to a clean, object-centered dataset such as ImageNet contributes additional performance gains. Thus, the reported success reflects both the learned invariances and properties of the training data.

The authors then propose learning from unstructured videos to obtain stronger viewpoint invariance. Compared with MOCOv2 trained on the same data, their representations perform better in the invariances measured and on downstream image classification and semantic segmentation. These findings connect representation quality to the particular variations the training process exposes.
neurips-2020-demystifying-contrastive-se.tldr: The paper identifies gaps in contrastive image invariances and uses unstructured video to improve viewpoint invariance and downstream performance.

paragraphs: An image can support several valid descriptions, so diverse captioning requires learning multiple possible text outputs for one visual input. This paper argues that earlier latent-variable approaches capture only the diversity present in their paired training examples. Descriptions attached to other images may contain useful contextual variation that those approaches do not fully exploit.

The proposed COS-CVAE separates its latent space into context and object components. This factorization lets the model use descriptions of similar contexts across different visual scenes. Context-based pseudo supervision provides an additional source of guidance for producing varied captions, drawing on relationships across the dataset rather than only each image's own paired descriptions.

The framework also extends to images containing novel objects and lacking paired captions in training. Evaluation uses both standard COCO and a held-out COCO dataset containing novel objects. The authors report significant gains in accuracy and diversity, indicating that the added contextual variation improves the range of captions without merely trading away their accuracy.
neurips-2020-diverse-image-captioning-wi.tldr: Separating context and object information lets a captioning model reuse contextual descriptions and improve caption accuracy and diversity.

paragraphs: Transfer learning starts with a model trained on one dataset and adapts it to another task. A common expectation is that a more accurate starting model will transfer better. This paper examines another property of the starting model: adversarial robustness. It asks whether models trained to resist adversarial changes can provide more useful representations for subsequent tasks.

The authors study adversarially robust ImageNet classifiers and compare their transfer performance with standard-trained counterparts. They find that robust models often transfer better even though they are less accurate on their original task. On a standard collection of downstream classification tasks, the robust classifiers yield improved accuracy after transfer.

This finding makes source-task accuracy an incomplete indicator of a model's usefulness for adaptation. Further analysis identifies additional differences between robust and standard models in transfer learning. The results support hypotheses that robustness improves feature representations, while the stated pattern remains that robust models often transfer better, rather than that robustness guarantees an advantage on every downstream task.
neurips-2020-do-adversarially-robust-ima.tldr: Adversarially robust ImageNet models often transfer better to classification tasks despite having lower accuracy on their original task.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether information about the image manifold can improve adversarial defenses. It considers a setting where this information is available, learning an approximate manifold with StyleGAN on an ImageNet subset. Projecting images onto it creates OM-ImageNet, where the manifold information is exact by construction.

Training against attacks restricted to that manifold improves normal accuracy and robustness to on-manifold attacks. However, this leaves perturbations outside the manifold unrepresented, and Lp attacks can still break the defense. The proposed Dual Manifold Adversarial Training addresses both directions by using adversarial perturbations in the model's latent space and in image space.

The authors report improved normal-image performance and robustness comparable to standard adversarial training against Lp attacks. They also observe better resistance to novel attacks involving global color shifts and image filtering, with similar improvements on natural images outside the learned manifold. These results support the potential value of manifold information under the studied conditions, rather than establishing protection against arbitrary attacks.
neurips-2020-dual-manifold-adversarial-r.tldr: Combining latent-space and image-space adversarial training improves accuracy and resistance to several attack types in the studied manifold-informed setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much information a message-passing graph neural network needs to distinguish graph structures. It introduces communication capacity, a measure of the information nodes can exchange during a forward pass. Capacity depends jointly on depth, message size, global state, and network width, bringing several architectural choices into one analysis.

The authors derive necessary capacity growth for the classification form of graph isomorphism: linear growth with node count for trees and quadratic growth for general connected graphs. These are lower bounds on the resources needed for distinguishing graphs. They address both worst-case and average-case behavior and apply with or without unique node features, including adaptive architectures.

The resulting bounds are up to two orders of magnitude tighter than those obtained through simpler arguments. An empirical study spanning 12 graph classification tasks and 420 networks finds strong agreement between observed performance and theoretical predictions. The work therefore connects limits on information exchange to practical architectural performance, even in a model family that is universal with unique node features.
neurips-2020-how-hard-is-to-distinguish-.tldr: Communication-capacity bounds quantify how message-passing graph networks must scale to distinguish trees and general connected graphs.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for inferring how animals update their behavior during learning. It estimates trial-by-trial changes in an animal's policy and separates a learning component from noise. This makes it possible to compare candidate learning rules and objectives, estimate different learning rates for policy parameters, and examine variation across animal cohorts.

After validation on simulated choices, the authors apply the framework to rats and mice learning perceptual decisions. For mice performing the International Brain Laboratory task, conventional REINFORCE accounts for an average of 30% of policy updates under the model. Adding baseline parameters raises the explained contribution to 92%, showing that these parameters substantially improve the modeled account of behavioral change.

The best-fitting learning rates and baseline values indicate that each trial's policy update does not follow the direction that maximizes expected reward. This conclusion concerns the inferred updates under the framework. The approach also exposes changes that normative learning rules miss, providing empirical descriptions of biological learning for neuroscience and machine learning.
neurips-2020-inferring-learning-rules-fr.tldr: A behavioral modeling framework infers animal learning updates and finds that baseline-augmented rules explain mouse policy changes substantially better.

paragraphs: A neural backdoor makes a model behave abnormally on triggered inputs even when it performs well on clean data. This paper targets a common feature of earlier backdoors: the same trigger pattern is reused across inputs. Such uniformity gives defenses a recurring pattern to detect and mitigate, motivating the authors to investigate triggers that depend on the input.

The proposed method uses an input-aware generator and a diversity loss to produce varying triggers. It also introduces a cross-trigger test to enforce nonreusability across inputs. The authors describe this as preventing backdoor verification through trigger reuse, making the relationship between a trigger and its particular input central to the attack.

Experiments across multiple datasets and attack scenarios report an efficient attack that bypasses the state-of-the-art defenses evaluated. Analysis with a neural network inspection tool further supports its stealthiness. The security finding is that defenses built around a shared trigger can be challenged by input-dependent patterns whose behavior does not transfer in the same way.
neurips-2020-input-aware-dynamic-backdoo.tldr: Input-dependent, nonreusable triggers let the proposed backdoor evade the defenses and inspection methods evaluated in the paper.

paragraphs: DIVE is a deep generative model for learning from video sequences with missing data. It tackles both filling in missing observations and predicting future frames. The central idea is to represent missingness explicitly alongside the factors describing the objects in a video, so incomplete observations become part of the representation-learning problem.

For each object, the model separates static appearance, dynamic appearance, pose, and missingness into distinct hidden factors. It also imputes the object's trajectory where observations are absent. This connects the representation of what an object looks like and how it changes with the task of reconstructing its unobserved behavior over time.

The authors evaluate DIVE on moving MNIST under several missing-data scenarios and report a substantial improvement over state-of-the-art baselines. They also present comparisons on the MOTSChallenge pedestrian dataset to demonstrate practical value in a more realistic setting. Together, these evaluations support explicitly modeling missingness and object-level factors when completing and forecasting incomplete videos.
neurips-2020-learning-disentangled-repre.tldr: DIVE separates object appearance, pose, and missingness to reconstruct incomplete video trajectories and predict future frames.

paragraphs: A local contrastive explanation shows how changing a few input features can move a black-box model's prediction to another class. A global transparent model, such as a decision tree or rule list, offers a broader account of predictions. This paper examines whether a transparent substitute can remain accurate while preserving the black box's local explanations.

Matching labels or black-box predictions does not by itself establish that the same contrastive explanations apply to both models. The authors introduce a local consistency metric to measure this relationship. It checks whether explanations derived for the black box are also applicable to the transparent surrogate, giving explanation agreement its own evaluation criterion.

Their method constructs custom Boolean features from the black box's local contrastive explanations and uses those features to train a transparent model. The resulting models achieve higher local consistency than other known strategies while retaining accuracy. The contribution connects local explanations to global model construction, rather than treating those two forms of interpretability as independent outputs.
neurips-2020-learning-global-transparent.tldr: Features derived from local contrastive explanations help train accurate transparent models that better preserve a black box's explanations.

paragraphs: Bregman divergences form a broad family of comparison measures that includes squared Euclidean distance and KL divergence. This paper asks how to learn an approximation to an arbitrary member of that family from supervision. The aim is to learn the comparison rule itself, giving metric learning access to a wider class of relationships.

The method works through the convex function that generates a Bregman divergence. It approximates that generating function with a piecewise linear function and develops a corresponding learning formulation and algorithm. This provides a structured way to learn divergences, along with theoretical bounds describing the quality of approximations available through the parameterization.

The authors also establish a generalization-error rate of O_p(m^(-1/2)) for metric learning in their framework. This matches the known rate for the less general Mahalanobis metric-learning setting. Empirical comparisons show good performance against existing metric-learning methods, particularly in clustering and ranking, supporting the usefulness of the broader family as well as its theoretical analysis.
neurips-2020-learning-to-approximate-a-b.tldr: Learning a piecewise linear convex generator enables supervised approximation of Bregman divergences with approximation and generalization guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies online convex optimization when a player has a limited number of opportunities to change actions. Over T rounds with fewer than K switches, it establishes minimax regret of order T divided by the square root of K. This characterizes the best achievable worst-case performance as the switching allowance changes.

The proof combines lower bounds with an algorithm that reaches the same scaling. In higher dimensions, an orthogonal-subspace argument gives a lower bound of T/sqrt(K). For one dimension, the authors introduce a relaxation called the fugal game to obtain the sharper constant in the bound T/sqrt(2K). A mini-batching algorithm supplies a dimension-independent upper bound of the matching order.

Together, these results resolve both the optimal rate and how to achieve it algorithmically. The same rate describes the switching regimes considered, unlike the discrete prediction-from-experts counterpart, which exhibits a phase transition between low and high switching allowances. The distinction shows that the continuous action setting has a different switching-performance relationship.
neurips-2020-minimax-regret-of-switching.tldr: Switching-constrained online convex optimization has minimax regret Θ(T/√K), with a matching mini-batching algorithm and no discrete-style phase transition.

paragraphs: A graph network should give a coherent result regardless of how the same graph is described. Traditionally, this requirement is expressed through equivariance to node permutations: relabeling nodes should change the representation in the corresponding way. This paper revisits the mathematical condition needed to make graph processing well-defined.

The authors show that a more general condition called naturality is sufficient. This opens a larger class of possible graph networks while preserving the required consistency across descriptions. They define both global and local natural graph networks. The local version has scalability comparable to conventional message-passing networks while allowing greater flexibility.

The paper also provides a practical instance using an equivariant parameterization of its message network and reports good performance on several benchmarks. Thus, the broader framework can still use equivariant components. Its contribution is both conceptual and architectural: it expands the conditions under which graph networks can be constructed and demonstrates a usable member of that expanded family.
neurips-2020-natural-graph-networks-90b6.tldr: Naturality provides a more general sufficient condition for well-defined graph networks, enabling flexible architectures with scalable local variants.

paragraphs: The paper considers finding a size-k configuration with high probability under a determinantal point process. Its target is the maximum-probability configuration, known as MAP inference. The online setting adds two important constraints: data can arrive in any order, and selected elements cannot later be discarded from the algorithm's local memory.

The authors give an efficient approximation algorithm whose memory footprint does not depend on the total length of the incoming stream. For a chosen additive tolerance η, its guarantee combines a multiplicative approximation factor of k raised to O(k) with additive error η. The guarantee therefore explicitly depends on the requested configuration size and allows the specified additive error.

The exponential dependence on k in the approximation factor is unavoidable even when all data are available offline, according to the paper. This situates the online result against a difficulty already present without streaming constraints. The result also directly yields a streaming algorithm with a better memory bound than existing results.
neurips-2020-online-map-inference-of-det.tldr: An online algorithm approximates size-k DPP MAP inference using memory independent of stream length, with explicit multiplicative and additive guarantees.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across users who communicate with a central server without exchanging their data samples. A single shared output, however, does not directly accommodate differences between users' data distributions. This paper instead seeks a shared starting model that each current or new user can adapt using one or a few gradient steps on local data.

The authors formulate that objective through Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning. The shared model is intended to support rapid personalization, so local adaptation becomes part of the learning goal. Building on this connection, they study a personalized version of Federated Averaging while retaining the central-server communication structure.

The theoretical analysis evaluates performance through gradient norms for non-convex losses. It also characterizes how that performance depends on similarity between user distributions, measured using distances including Total Variation and 1-Wasserstein. This links the behavior of the personalization method to the degree of data heterogeneity, providing a mathematical account of an issue that motivates personalized federated learning in the first place.
neurips-2020-personalized-federated-lear.tldr: A MAML-based variant of Federated Averaging learns a shared initialization for local personalization and analyzes how user-distribution differences affect performance.

paragraphs: Domain-adaptive semantic segmentation seeks accurate pixel labels in a target domain using annotations from a different source domain. This paper argues that methods based on global adversarial alignment overlook relationships between individual pixels. Reducing an overall domain discrepancy can therefore miss information useful for making pixel features more discriminative.

The proposed approach builds cycle associations between source and target pixel pairs. It then strengthens these connections contrastively, using pixel-level relationships to reduce the domain gap. The key change is the granularity of the transfer mechanism: it explicitly links pixels across domains instead of considering only their global discrepancy.

Experiments on GTAV-to-Cityscapes and SYNTHIA-to-Cityscapes demonstrate effectiveness and favorable performance against previous state-of-the-art methods. The approach trains end to end in a single stage and adds no parameters. Those properties make the proposed association mechanism attractive as a broader framework for domain adaptation research, which the authors present as an expected use rather than an established result across all settings.
neurips-2020-pixel-level-cycle-associati.tldr: Contrastively strengthened pixel-level cycle associations improve domain-adaptive segmentation without adding model parameters.

paragraphs: Few-shot object detection asks a model to recognize and locate new object classes from only a few annotated examples. This paper identifies a problem in early approaches that emphasize positive candidate regions while discarding regions that are negative for the class. That simplification loses information the authors regard as essential for learning a useful embedding space.

The proposed method represents both positive and negative examples in a metric-learning framework. It builds on RepMet, adding modules that encode negative information during training and testing. A corresponding inference scheme uses both kinds of representatives when making predictions, so negatives influence the final decision as well as the learned representation.

Hard negatives are particularly relevant because they supply challenging distinctions for the embedding to capture. Experiments on ImageNet-LOC and PASCAL VOC report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art few-shot detection solutions. The findings support treating negative evidence as an explicit part of the detector's learning and prediction process when examples of new classes are scarce.
neurips-2020-restoring-negative-informat.tldr: Explicit positive and negative representatives improve few-shot object detection by restoring negative evidence during training and prediction.

paragraphs: Training data may represent a different input distribution from the data a model will encounter in use, creating covariate shift. Common correction methods estimate a ratio between training and target probability densities. This paper focuses on the practical difficulties of that approach: parameter tuning and instability across datasets.

The authors propose using empirical cumulative distribution estimates of the target distribution instead. These estimates summarize accumulated probability rather than directly estimating the density ratio used by the conventional approaches discussed. The method rigorously generalizes an earlier idea by Vapnik and Izmailov, providing an alternative mathematical route for correcting sampling bias.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show more robust predictions without reliance on parameter tuning. Classification performance is similar to that of current state-of-the-art techniques. The reported benefit is therefore stability and reduced tuning requirements while maintaining comparable classification results. This matters because correcting a distribution mismatch is more useful when the correction itself behaves reliably across the datasets being evaluated.
neurips-2020-robust-correction-of-sampli.tldr: Empirical cumulative distributions provide a covariate-shift correction with more robust predictions, no parameter tuning, and comparable classification performance.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether large neural networks could be trained using computing resources contributed by volunteers. Its motivation is the expense of the infrastructure used for increasingly large models. A sufficiently large collection of ordinary computers could offer substantial raw computing power, but conventional distributed training cannot efficiently use that power under the conditions considered.

The proposed Learning@home paradigm is designed for many participants with poor connectivity. The title frames the approach around decentralized mixtures of experts. The central systems question is how a training design can accommodate the communication conditions of crowdsourced resources, since aggregate computing power alone does not establish that training will be effective.

The authors analyze performance, reliability, and architectural constraints and compare the paradigm with existing distributed training techniques. This makes the work an investigation of what crowdsourced training requires as well as a proposed approach. The abstract presents volunteer-powered training as a possibility to pursue, without claiming that a large volunteer deployment has already achieved it.
neurips-2020-towards-crowdsourced-traini.tldr: Learning@home explores decentralized training designed to use large numbers of poorly connected volunteer computers.

paragraphs: Many contrastive learning methods teach representations to agree across different views of the same instance. Invariance Propagation instead targets variation between different instances of the same category. The goal is to learn features that capture shared category information despite differences between individual examples, extending the scope of the invariance being learned.

The method recursively discovers semantically consistent samples within the same high-density regions of representation space. It then emphasizes hard positive samples when maximizing agreement with an anchor. These positives provide more variation within a class, encouraging the representation to capture more abstract commonalities than agreement between closely related views alone.

With a ResNet-50 backbone, the method achieves 71.3% top-1 accuracy for ImageNet linear classification and 78.2% top-5 accuracy when fine-tuned using only 1% of labels, surpassing previous results. It also reports state-of-the-art results on Places205 and Pascal VOC linear classification and transfer to small datasets. These findings support the usefulness of discovering cross-instance relationships without supervised category labels.
neurips-2020-unsupervised-representation.tldr: Invariance Propagation discovers related instances and emphasizes hard positives to learn category-level invariances without supervision.

paragraphs: This paper improves a matching-based approach to semi-supervised video object segmentation. Such approaches store features in a bank and use them to match and classify image regions. As a video continues, that bank can keep growing. The authors identify organization of this accumulated information as an underexplored source of inefficiency.

Their framework updates the feature bank adaptively, incorporating new features while removing obsolete ones. This makes information management an explicit part of the segmentation method. The bank can respond to new observations without simply preserving every feature accumulated earlier, addressing the storage design problem described in the paper.

A second part targets regions where segmentation is uncertain. The authors introduce a confidence loss and a fine-grained segmentation module to improve accuracy in those areas. Together, the changes address both the information used for matching and the refinement of uncertain predictions. On public benchmarks, the complete algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combined framework's effectiveness.
neurips-2020-video-object-segmentation-w.tldr: Adaptive feature-bank updates and targeted refinement of uncertain regions improve matching-based video object segmentation.
